name: GO Classes CS Test Series | C programming | Subject Wise Test 2

question.text:
Which figure correctly diagrams the related contents of memory after this code fragment executes?

int main() {
    int a[] = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9};
    int i = 1;
    if (i < sizeof(a)/sizeof(a[0]) && a[i] % 3 != 0) {
        a[i + 1] = 3;
        i+= 2;
    }
    // Print values of array a and variable i
    return 0;
}

int messUp(int a, int b) {
    int c = 4;
    a++;
    b--;
    return a + c;
}
int main() {
    int a = 1, b = 2, c = 3;
    a = messUp(b, a);
    printf("%d\n", a + b + c);
    return 0;
}


Which one of the following shows what the program displays when executed?

  1. $11$
     
  2. $12$
     
  3. $13$
     
  4. $123$

For which values of an integer named choice do these two code fragments produce the same results?

//Code1

if (choice == 1) duel();
else if (choice == 2) train();
else forfeit();
//Code2

switch (choice) {
  case 1: duel(); break;
  case 2: train();
  default: forfeit();
}
  1. choice less than or equal to 1
  2. choice equal to 2
  3. choice greater than or equal to 3
A. i, ii, and iii
B. i and iii only
C. i and ii only
D. ii and iii only

Consider the following C function:

char mystery(char n) {
    int p = 1;
    while (p * 2 <= n) {
        p *= 2;
    }
    return p;
}


What will be printed when the following line is executed?

printf("\%d\n", mystery(17));
  1. $16$
     
  2. $17$
     
  3. $32$
     
  4. $8$

What will be the output of the following C program?

#include <stdio.h>

void count(int n)
{
    static int d = 1;
    printf("%d", n);
    printf("%d", d);
    d++;
    if (n > 1)
        count(n - 1);
    printf("\n");
}

int main()
{
    count(3);
    return 0;
}

 

  1. $31\newline 22\newline 13$
     
  2. $31\newline 21\newline 11$
     
  3. $31\newline 22\newline 11$
     
  4. $31\newline 21\newline 13$

What will be the final value of $i$ after executing the following $C$ code?
 

int main() {
    int i = 0;
    if (i++ && i == 1 || i++)
        printf("Yes\n");
    else
        printf("No\n");

}

How many distinct outputs are possible when the following C program is executed?

int f1() { printf("1"); return 1; }
int f2() { printf("2"); return 2; }
int f3() { printf("3"); return 3; }
int main() {
    int x = printf("%d", f1() + f2() + f3());
    return 0;
}
  1. $1$
     
  2. $3$
     
  3. $6$
     
  4. $9$

Consider the following recursive C function:

void recursionMystery2(int a, char c) {
    if (a != 0) {
        printf("%c", c);
        if (a % 2 == 0) {
            printf("O");
            recursionMystery2(a - 1, c - 1);
        } else {
            recursionMystery2(a - 1, c + 1);
            printf("R");
        }
    }
}


What will be the output of the following function call?

recursionMystery2(3, 'd');
  1. deOdRR
     
  2. dOeOdRR
     
  3. dOeRdR
     
  4. deOdRr

Consider the following C code:

typedef struct { int x, y; } Point;
typedef struct { Point* p; } Box;
int rotate(int a, Box* b) {
    int t = a;
    a = b->p->x;
    b->p->x = b->p->y;
    b->p->y = t;
    return a;
}
int main() {
    int a = 3;
    Point* p = malloc(sizeof(Point));
    p->x = 10; p->y = 5;
    Box b1 = {p};
    a = rotate(a, &b1);
    printf("%d\n", a);
    free(p);
    return 0;
}


What is the value printed by printf?

  1. $3$
     
  2. $5$
     
  3. $10$
     
  4. Garbage value

What will be the output of the following C program?
 

#include <stdio.h>
struct Block {
    int mat[2][2];
};
int main() {
    struct Block b[] = {
        {{{1, 2}, {3, 4} }},
        {{{5,6}, {7, 8} }}
    };
    struct Block *ptr = b;
    
    printf("%d", (*((ptr + 1))->mat)[0]);
    return 0;
}
  1. $5$
     
  2. $6$
     
  3. $7$
     
  4. Compilation Error

Consider the following condition where n is an integer variable:

Which one of the following number lines correctly shows in bold the range of n where the condition evaluates to TRUE ?

Note: Filled circles represent points that are included in the range, and hollow circles represent points that are not included.

Which choice best represents the call stack at the point of execution when the stack has the greatest number of active function calls (deepest call stack)?

int main() {
    methodA();
    methodC();
    return 0;
}
void methodA() {
    printf("A");
    methodB();
}
void methodB() {
    methodC();
    printf("B");
    methodD();
}
void methodC() {
    methodD();
    printf("C");
}
void methodD() {
    printf("D");
}
  1. main $\rightarrow$ methodA $\rightarrow$ methodB $\rightarrow$ methodC $\rightarrow$ methodD $\rightarrow$ methodD
     
  2. main $\rightarrow$ methodA $\rightarrow$ methodD $\rightarrow$ methodC $\rightarrow$ methodB $\rightarrow$ methodD $\rightarrow$ methodA
     
  3. main $\rightarrow$ methodA $\rightarrow$ methodD $\rightarrow$ methodC $\rightarrow$ methodB $\rightarrow$ methodD
     
  4. main $\rightarrow$ methodA $\rightarrow$ methodB $\rightarrow$ methodC $\rightarrow$ methodD

What will be the output of the following C program?

#include <stdio.h>
int fun(int *a, int i) {
    return a[i] + i;
}
int main() {
    int arr[] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
    int i = 1;
    printf("%d\n", fun(arr, i++) + fun(arr, ++i));
    return 0;
}
  1. $6$
     
  2. $63$
     
  3. Undefined Behavior
     
  4. $60$

What will be the output of the following C program?
 

void update(int **q) {
    *q = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    **q = 50;
}
int main() {
    int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 10;
    update(&p);
    printf("%d\n", *p);
    return 0;
}
  1. $10$
  2. $50$
  3. The value depends on system architecture ($32$-bit vs $64$-bit)
  4. Program compiles but prints a garbage value

Which of the following statements about memory leaks is/are correct?
Select ALL valid options.

  1. A program will not be able to access memory that has been leaked.
  2. Leaked memory is no longer part of the heap segment.
  3. Leaked memory cannot be freed, which may cause the program's memory usage to grow over time.
  4. Every instance of memory leak always results in undefined program behaviour.

What will be the output of the following C program?
 

#include <stdio.h>
int mystery(int n) {
    static int x = 1;
    if (n <= 0)
        return 0;
    x++;
    return mystery(n-1) + x;
}
int main() {
    printf("%d\n", mystery(3));
    return 0;
}

Consider the following recursive function in C :

int recursionMystery1(int a, int b) {
    if (a < b) return a;
    return recursionMystery1(a - b, b);
}


What is the return value of the following function call recursionMystery1 $(10,4)$ ?

Consider the following C function:  

bool findSomething(int a[], int b[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        bool found = false;
        for (int j = 0; j < length; j++) {
            if (a[i] == b[j]) {
                found = true;
                break;

            }
        }
        if (!found)
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}


Precondition: Arrays $a$ and $b$ have equal length.

Which best describes what the function findSomething does? It returns true only if:

  1. Arrays $a$ and $b$ contain identical elements in the same order.
     
  2. Arrays $a$ and $b$ contain identical elements in reverse order.
     
  3. Arrays $a$ and $b$ are permutations of each other.
     
  4. Every element of array $a$ is also in $b$, and every element of array $b$ is also in $a$

if (lst == NULL) return;
